title: Productivity & Time Management at Work
subtitle: Set clear work goals, plan focused time in Google Calendar, control email and WhatsApp interruptions and prove your improvement with real numbers.
description: A practical course for women in jobs and businesses who are busy all day but struggle to finish the work that matters. You will set goals with SMART and OKRs, build a task system in Google Tasks and Keep, time-block your day, batch messages, delegate and protect your pace. You finish with a tested, measured improvement and a 90-day plan.
outcomes: Write work goals as SMART goals and quarterly OKRs, and trace weekly tasks back to them
Measure your working baseline: focused hours, interruptions and time spent on results
Run a trusted task system in Google Tasks and Keep and a time-blocked day in Google Calendar
Cut email and WhatsApp interruptions with batching, Gmail tools and WhatsApp Business features
Delegate with a clear brief and protect a sustainable pace with a weekly review and scorecard
Test one change against your baseline and present the before-and-after results
audience: Women in paid work, small businesses or community organisations who want to get more of the right work done without working longer hours.
tools: A smartphone (Android or iPhone) with a Google account
Google Calendar, Google Tasks and Google Keep (free)
WhatsApp, and WhatsApp Business if you serve customers
Gmail and Google Sheets (free), or a notebook and pen if data is limited
A phone timer for Pomodoro sessions

modules.title: Foundations: Outcomes, Goals and Your Working Baseline
modules.overview: Productivity at work is about finishing the work that moves results, not about looking busy. In this module you learn the difference between output and activity, write work goals with SMART and OKRs, and measure how your working hours and attention are really spent today.

lessons.title: Output, not hours: what productivity means at work
objectives: Distinguish output (results) from activity (effort and motion) in your own job or business
Identify the three to five results your role or business is really paid for
Recognise the difference between deep work and shallow work
Explain why a schedule built around meetings breaks up focused work

blocks.text: Ask ten people at a Lagos office or a market stall how their week went and many will say "very busy". Busy describes **activity**: messages answered, calls taken, meetings attended. Productivity describes **output**: the results your job or business exists to deliver. A customer service officer's output might be complaints resolved. A caterer's output is orders delivered on time and paid for. A head teacher's output includes lessons taught well and parents kept informed. This course is about growing output without adding hours.

blocks.name: time-management
blocks.alt: A woman standing beside a large clock and a task board
blocks.caption: Time management at work starts by asking which results your hours should buy.

blocks.text: Find what you are really paid for

Every role has a short list of **key results areas**: the few outcomes that, if done well, make everything else easier. Most people can name three to five. Write yours as results, not tasks. "Send invoices" is a task. "Every client invoiced within two days of delivery and paid within 30 days" is a result. When you know your results areas, you can judge any request by one question: does this move one of my results?

head: Role (for example)
Activity that feels productive
Output that actually counts
rows: Sales officer at a bank branch
Replying to every WhatsApp message instantly
New accounts opened and loans disbursed
Chatting with walk-in visitors all afternoon
Garments finished, collected and paid for by the promised date
Reports submitted on time, files easy to find, events running smoothly
Students understanding and passing the topic

blocks.text: Deep work and shallow work

The writer and computer science professor **Cal Newport** popularised two useful labels in his book *Deep Work* (2016). **Deep work** is focused, demanding work that needs your full attention and creates real value: writing a proposal, designing a new product, preparing a budget, planning a training. **Shallow work** is easier, often logistical work that you can do while distracted: forwarding a file, confirming a meeting time, updating a register. Both are needed. The problem is that shallow work arrives all day by itself, while deep work only happens if you protect time for it.

A practical test: if a smart new colleague could do the task well after one week of training, it is probably shallow. If it needs your experience, judgement or creativity, it is probably deep. Most people find their key results depend on deep work, yet their days are filled with shallow work.
Why meetings cut a day into pieces

In a well known 2009 essay, the programmer and investor **Paul Graham** described the "maker's schedule" and the "manager's schedule". A manager's day is divided into hour slots, and a meeting simply fills one slot. A maker, someone who writes, designs, plans or builds, needs long unbroken stretches. One meeting at 11 a.m. can spoil a whole morning for a maker, because the time before it is too short to start something serious. Many women in work and business are both makers and managers, so the skill is to group meetings and calls together and keep separate blocks for making.

blocks.title: A busy day and a productive day
items: Busy day
Productive day
right: Starts with the day's key task
Calls grouped into one afternoon block
Two or three important tasks finished
blocks.caption: The two days can have the same number of hours; the difference is how attention is directed.

blocks.title: Worked example: naming results for a small business
blocks.context: For example, Amaka runs a small printing business in Onitsha with one assistant. She says she works from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. but profit is flat.
steps: She lists everything she did on Tuesday: 14 tasks, including 3 hours on WhatsApp chats and 1 hour going to the bank.
She writes her results areas: (1) jobs delivered on time and correct, (2) new corporate clients, (3) cash collected, (4) a trained assistant.
She marks each Tuesday task with the result it served. Only 5 of 14 tasks served a result; none served "new corporate clients".
She decides that every weekday from 9 to 10:30 a.m. is for deep work on one results area, starting with writing a short company profile to send to schools and churches.
blocks.result: Amaka now has a clear test for her time. Within the week she sends her profile to six potential clients, work she had postponed for months while staying "busy".

blocks.text: Three questions to ask every morning

items: **Which result matters most today?** Pick one results area and one task that moves it.
**When will I do it?** Give it a time, ideally in the hours when your mind is freshest, before messages pile up.
**What will I not do?** Name one low-value activity you will skip or shorten so the important task gets its time.

blocks.title: Productivity is not working longer
blocks.text: Adding hours is the most expensive way to increase output, and it is not sustainable. This course will help you get more of the right work done inside the hours you already have, and protect your rest while you do it (Module 3).

takeaways: Activity is effort; output is results. Measure yourself by output.
Name three to five key results areas for your role or business.
Deep work creates most of the value but needs protected time.
Group meetings and calls so they do not break up making time.

activity.title: Write your key results areas
steps: List every task you did on your last full working day.
Write three to five key results areas for your job or business, as outcomes, not tasks.
Mark each task from your list with the result it served, or with an X if it served none.
Label each task D (deep) or S (shallow).
Choose one deep task linked to a result that you will do first thing tomorrow.
activity.evidence: A photo or screenshot of your task list with results areas, D/S labels and X marks.

lessons.title: Setting work goals with SMART goals and OKRs
objectives: Rewrite a vague work goal as a SMART goal
Write one objective with three measurable key results (an OKR)
Choose when a SMART goal or an OKR fits better
Break a quarterly key result into weekly actions

blocks.text: A goal turns your results areas into a target with a finish line. Without one, every week feels the same and it is hard to say no to anything. Two methods are widely used in workplaces around the world: **SMART goals** for clear individual targets, and **OKRs** (Objectives and Key Results) for ambitious targets that a person, team or business works towards over a quarter.

blocks.name: goals
blocks.alt: A person placing a flag on a target
blocks.caption: A good work goal has a clear finish line you can measure.

blocks.text: SMART goals

The SMART idea was published by **George T. Doran** in the journal *Management Review* in 1981. Today the letters are usually read as: **Specific** (what exactly), **Measurable** (a number or clear sign of completion), **Achievable** (possible with your time and resources), **Relevant** (linked to a results area) and **Time-bound** (a deadline).

head: Vague goal
SMART version
rows: Reply to every customer enquiry on the business WhatsApp within 2 working hours, from 1 March to 31 March
Sign 3 new corporate clients for office printing by 30 June, by visiting 4 businesses each week
Submit the monthly programme report by the 5th working day of each month for the next 3 months

blocks.text: OKRs: an objective plus key results

OKRs grew out of the management practice of **Andy Grove** at Intel. **John Doerr**, who learned the method at Intel, introduced it to Google in its early years and later wrote the book *Measure What Matters* (2018). An OKR has two parts:

items: **Objective**: what you want to achieve, written in plain, inspiring words. It has no number. For example: "Make our bakery the first choice for office events in Wuse."

**Key results**: usually three to five measurable signs that show you reached the objective. Each has a number and a date. For example: "Deliver 20 office orders this quarter", "Get 10 written reviews from office clients", "Repeat orders from at least 5 offices".
**Initiatives**: the actions you take to move the key results, such as building a price list for corporate packs. These are tasks, not key results.

blocks.text: A key result describes an outcome, not an activity. "Send 50 flyers" is an activity; "Get 10 new office enquiries" is a result. At Google, OKRs are often deliberately ambitious and scored from 0 to 1 at the end of the quarter, so reaching most but not all of a stretch key result can still be a good outcome. If you use OKRs with a manager, agree in advance whether a key result is a firm commitment or a stretch target.

blocks.title: From objective to this week
items: Objective (the what)
Key results (numbers, dates)
Initiatives (projects)
Weekly actions
Today's task
blocks.caption: Each layer serves the one above it, so today's task can always be traced back to the objective.

blocks.text: Which one should you use?

Use a **SMART goal** when the target is personal, clear and must be fully achieved, such as a report deadline or a sales quota set by your employer. Use an **OKR** when you want to stretch, when several people are involved, or when you need a few measures to describe one bigger aim. You can combine them: each key result should itself be specific, measurable and time-bound.

blocks.title: Worked example: a quarterly OKR for a fashion business
blocks.context: For example, Halima designs and sells women's clothing in Kano through Instagram and WhatsApp. Sales have been uneven. It is the start of the July to September quarter.
steps: Objective: "Build steady monthly sales from returning customers."
Key result 1: 40 repeat customers by 30 September (she had about 15 in the last quarter, from her sales book).
Key result 2: Average order value of 25,000 naira (approximate) or more, up from about 18,000 naira.
Key result 3: 4 new collections announced on schedule, one every three weeks.
Initiatives: start a broadcast list of past buyers, create a matching scarf and bag add-on, plan the collection calendar.
Weekly action for week 1: tidy her contact list and label every past buyer, 1 hour on Monday and Thursday.
blocks.result: Halima can check her progress every Friday against three numbers instead of a general hope for "more sales". At the end of September she scores each key result and sets the next quarter's OKR.

blocks.text: Common mistakes when writing goals

items: **Too many key results**: ten measures for one objective means none gets attention. Keep three to five.
**Measuring effort instead of result**: "work harder on marketing" cannot be checked. Ask: what number would change if this worked?
**No baseline**: "increase repeat customers" means little if you do not know how many you have now. Look in your sales book or records first.
**Set and forget**: a goal written in January and read again in December has not guided anything. Check key results weekly.

blocks.title: Keep it to a few
blocks.text: One to three objectives per quarter is plenty for one person. More than that and the goals compete for the same hours, which brings back the busy-but-stuck feeling the goals were meant to fix.

takeaways: SMART: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound.
An OKR is one inspiring objective plus a few measurable key results.
Key results measure outcomes; initiatives are the actions you take.
Trace each weekly action back to a key result.

activity.title: Write your quarter's goal
steps: Pick the results area from Lesson 1 that most needs progress.
Write one objective in plain words without a number.
Add three key results, each with a number and a date.
Check each key result against SMART and rewrite any that describe activity instead of outcome.
List two initiatives and one action you will take this week.
activity.evidence: Your written OKR (objective, three key results, initiatives, first weekly action) saved in Google Keep or on paper and photographed.

lessons.title: Your working baseline: a three-day work log and interruption count
objectives: Keep a simple work log for three working days
Count and classify interruptions by source
Calculate your real focused hours and your planned capacity
Identify your biggest workplace time drain with evidence

blocks.text: Before you change how you work, you need a starting measurement, called a **baseline**. Without it, you cannot tell later whether a new method helped. This lesson uses a short work log focused on three things: what you worked on, how long you stayed focused, and what pulled you away. You will use these numbers again in Module 4 for your before-and-after comparison.

blocks.name: work-time
blocks.alt: A person at a desk checking the time while working
blocks.caption: A baseline shows how your working hours and attention are really spent today.

blocks.text: Set up the log

Use a page in a notebook, a Google Keep note or a simple Google Sheet with five columns. Record in blocks of 30 minutes, or each time you switch task, whichever comes first. Keep it honest: the log is for you, not for your manager.
Classify your interruptions
An interruption is anything that stops the task you chose and makes you switch to another. Give each one a source code so patterns appear:

items: **W**: WhatsApp or SMS message you opened
**E**: email notification you checked
**C**: phone call
**P**: a person at your desk or shop counter
**S**: self-interruption, such as picking up the phone "just to check" or jumping to an easier task

blocks.text: Self-interruptions surprise many people. If most of your tally marks are S, the fix is about habits and phone settings. If most are P, it is about agreements with colleagues or customers. If most are W or E, Module 2 Lesson 3 will help directly.
Calculate your numbers

items: **Focused deep-work hours**: add up only the blocks marked Deep that had zero or one interruption. Divide by three for a daily average.
**Interruptions per day**: add all tally marks and divide by three.
**Time on results**: add the hours linked to a results area, divide by total working hours and turn it into a percentage.
**Fixed commitments**: total the hours in meetings, set duties (such as opening the shop or school runs during work hours) and travel.
**Planned capacity**: working hours minus fixed commitments minus a buffer of about 20 percent for the unexpected. This is how much you can realistically plan into a day.

blocks.title: From log to baseline
items: Log 3 working days
Tally interruptions by source
Total deep-work hours
Work out planned capacity
Name the biggest drain
blocks.caption: Three days of honest logging give you the numbers you will compare against at the end of the course.

blocks.title: Worked example: an office baseline
blocks.context: For example, Funke is a programme officer at an NGO in Ibadan. She works 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., 8 hours a day, and feels she never has time to write donor reports.
steps: Over three days she logs 24 hours. Blocks marked Deep with zero or one interruption total 3 hours, so her daily average is 1 hour of focused deep work.
She tallies 69 interruptions in three days, an average of 23 per day: W 31, P 18, S 14, C 6.
Hours linked to a results area total 13 out of 24, so 54 percent of her time is on results.
Fixed commitments: 2 hours of meetings a day on average. Capacity: 8 minus 2 is 6 hours; minus a 20 percent buffer (about 1.2 hours) leaves about 4.8 hours she can plan.
Her biggest drain, with evidence: WhatsApp (31 interruptions), mostly from a staff group chat that is busy all day.
blocks.result: Funke's baseline is: 1 focused hour a day, 23 interruptions a day, 54 percent of time on results, about 4.8 plannable hours. Her first target is the staff group chat.

blocks.title: Do not plan to 100 percent
blocks.text: If your plan fills every working hour, the first urgent request breaks the whole day. Planning to your real capacity, with a buffer, is what makes a plan believable. Many people find their daily to-do list has two or three times more work than their capacity allows.
Reading your results honestly

Look at your numbers before deciding what to change. Low deep-work hours with many W or E marks point to message habits. Low deep-work hours with few interruptions but many meetings point to a calendar problem. A low percentage of time on results with few interruptions often means unclear priorities: you are working steadily, but on the wrong things. Pick the one pattern that costs you most. Trying to fix everything at once usually means nothing changes.

blocks.title: Privacy at work
blocks.text: If you log in an office, keep client names and confidential details out of the log. Write "Client A report" rather than the client's name, especially if you use a shared device.

takeaways: A baseline lets you prove later that a change worked.
Tally interruptions by source: WhatsApp, email, calls, people, self.
Count focused deep-work hours, not just hours at work.
Plan to your real capacity with a buffer, not to every hour.

activity.title: Run your three-day baseline
steps: Set up a five-column log in a notebook, Google Keep or Google Sheets.
Log three normal working days in 30-minute blocks or at each task switch.
Tally interruptions with the codes W, E, C, P, S.
Calculate deep-work hours per day, interruptions per day, percentage of time on results and planned capacity.
Write one sentence naming your biggest time drain and the evidence for it.
activity.evidence: Your three-day log plus a baseline summary card with the four numbers and your named time drain (keep it for Module 4).

quiz.q: Ngozi spent Monday replying to 120 messages and attending three meetings, but her proposal is still unwritten. What best describes her day?
options: High output, because she was busy all day
High activity but low output on her key result
Deep work, because meetings need concentration
A productive day, because she answered everyone
quiz.explain: Messages and meetings are activity. Her key result, the proposal, did not move, so output was low.

quiz.q: Which of these is a key result rather than an initiative?
quiz.explain: A key result is a measurable outcome with a date. The others are actions (initiatives) that might help achieve it.

quiz.q: Which goal meets all the SMART criteria?
options: Send every client invoice within 2 working days of delivery from 1 May to 31 July
quiz.explain: It is specific, measurable (2 working days), achievable, relevant to cash collection, and has a clear time frame.

quiz.q: Funke works 8 hours a day with 2 hours of fixed meetings. Using a 20 percent buffer, roughly how many hours can she plan?
quiz.explain: 8 minus 2 leaves 6 hours. A 20 percent buffer is 1.2 hours, leaving about 4.8 hours of plannable work.

quiz.q: Most of Kemi's interruption tally marks are coded S (self-interruption). What is the most useful first fix?
options: Ask colleagues to stop visiting her desk
Change her phone habits and settings during focus time
Ask her manager for fewer meetings
quiz.explain: Self-interruptions come from her own checking habits, so phone settings and habits are the right lever. The other fixes target other sources.

quiz.q: Why does one meeting at 11 a.m. often damage a morning of writing or planning work?
options: Meetings are always a waste of time
Writing should only be done at night
It splits the morning into pieces too short to start demanding work
quiz.explain: Paul Graham's maker's schedule idea: makers need long unbroken blocks, and a mid-morning meeting breaks the time before it into a short, less useful slot.

modules.title: Guided Practice: Task Systems, Time Blocks and Message Control
modules.overview: Now you build the working system. You set up one trusted place for every task using Google Tasks and Keep, plan focused time in Google Calendar with time blocking, Pomodoro and batching, and take control of email and WhatsApp so they stop running your day.

lessons.title: A trusted task system: capture, clarify and organise with Google Tasks and Keep
objectives: Describe the five steps of the Getting Things Done (GTD) method
Capture every work commitment into one inbox instead of your memory
Turn vague items into clear next actions
Set up lists in Google Tasks and notes in Google Keep that you will actually use

blocks.text: Many people keep their work in their heads, on scraps of paper, in WhatsApp chats starred "for later" and in half-remembered promises made in meetings. The result is a constant feeling of something forgotten. **David Allen**, author of *Getting Things Done* (first published in 2001), argues that the mind is for having ideas, not holding them. His method, usually called **GTD**, gives every commitment a home outside your head so you can focus on one thing at a time.

blocks.name: add-tasks
blocks.alt: A person adding items to a large task list
blocks.caption: Every work commitment goes into one trusted list, not into your memory.

blocks.text: The five steps of GTD

blocks.title: The GTD workflow
items: Capture
Clarify
Organise
Reflect
Engage
blocks.caption: Collect everything, decide what each item means, put it in the right list, review it weekly, then do the work.

items: **Capture**: collect anything that has your attention (requests, ideas, promises) into an inbox. One inbox is best.

**Clarify**: for each item ask "Is it actionable?" If not, delete it, file it for reference or put it on a someday list. If yes, decide the very next physical action. If that action takes less than two minutes, do it now.

**Organise**: put actions where they belong: a next-actions list, a calendar (for things fixed to a date and time), a waiting-for list (things others owe you) or a projects list (outcomes needing more than one step).
**Reflect**: review the lists regularly, especially in a weekly review (Module 3, Lesson 3).
**Engage**: choose what to do now based on where you are, the time and energy you have, and your priorities.

blocks.text: Next actions: the key skill

Items such as "staff welfare" or "Lagos client" sit on lists for weeks because they are not actions. A **next action** starts with a verb and is something you could do right away: "Call Mrs Bello to confirm the venue", "Draft three questions for the staff welfare survey", "Email the Lagos client the revised quote". A **project** is any outcome that needs more than one action, such as "End-of-year staff party held". Keep the project on a projects list and always have at least one next action for it.
Setting it up in Google Tasks and Google Keep

Both apps are free with a Google account, work on Android and iPhone, and sync with a computer. **Google Tasks** is best for actions: each task can have a due date, a time, notes, subtasks and a repeat setting, and tasks with dates show in Google Calendar. You can also open Tasks from the side panel in Gmail and turn an email into a task. **Google Keep** is best for capture and reference: quick notes, checklists, voice notes, photos of documents, labels and reminders.

head: Where
What goes there
Example
rows: "Ask Tunde about delivery van" typed in 5 seconds
What others owe you, with the date you asked
Printer quote from Emeka, asked 3 June
Only things tied to a day or time
Bank account details for suppliers, price lists

blocks.title: Worked example: clearing a head full of tasks
blocks.context: For example, Grace is an operations manager at a logistics company in Port Harcourt. On Monday morning she feels overwhelmed and cannot say what is on her plate.
steps: Capture: in 15 minutes she writes 31 items into a Keep note, including items from her notebook, WhatsApp starred messages and two sticky notes.
Clarify: 4 items are not actionable (she deletes 3 and files 1 as reference). 6 take under two minutes, so she does them on the spot, finishing in about 10 minutes.
Of the remaining 21, she turns 13 into next actions in Google Tasks, 3 into a Waiting-for list with dates, and recognises 5 as projects, each with one next action.
Organise: she moves 2 items with fixed times (a vendor visit and a vehicle inspection) into Google Calendar.
Engage: she chooses the next action that serves her top key result: "Draft new delivery route for Trans-Amadi customers".
blocks.result: In about 45 minutes, 31 floating worries became 13 clear actions, 5 named projects and 3 tracked follow-ups. Grace starts the week knowing exactly what to do first.

blocks.title: One inbox, not five
blocks.text: If you capture into Keep, a notebook, WhatsApp "message yourself" and email drafts, you will forget to check some of them. Choose one main capture tool and, at most, one backup such as a small notebook for times your phone is off.

blocks.title: Data privacy
blocks.text: Do not store passwords, BVN, account PINs or customers' personal data in Keep notes. Use your employer's approved systems for confidential information, and protect your phone with a screen lock.

takeaways: Get commitments out of your head and into one trusted inbox.
Clarify every item: delete, file, do now (under two minutes) or list as a next action.
Next actions start with a verb; projects need at least one next action.
Google Tasks for actions, Google Keep for capture and reference, Calendar only for fixed times.

activity.title: Build your task system
steps: Do a 15-minute capture: write every work commitment into one Google Keep note or notebook page.
Clarify each item: delete, file, do now if under two minutes, or write a next action.
Create three lists in Google Tasks: Next actions, Waiting for, Projects.
Move date-specific items into Google Calendar.
Pick one next action that serves your OKR and do it today.
activity.evidence: Screenshots of your three Google Tasks lists and a count of how many items you captured, completed in under two minutes and organised.

lessons.title: Time blocking, Pomodoro and batching in Google Calendar
objectives: Build a time-blocked workday in Google Calendar
Run focused work sessions using the Pomodoro Technique
Batch similar shallow tasks into one block
Adjust a time-blocked plan when the day changes

blocks.text: A task list says **what** to do. A calendar says **when**. Time blocking joins the two: you give each important task a specific slot in your calendar, like an appointment with yourself. Cal Newport recommends planning every minute of the workday in blocks, then re-planning when things change. You do not need to be that strict. Blocking even your top two or three tasks makes a large difference, because a task with a time is much more likely to happen than a task on a list.

blocks.name: online-calendar
blocks.alt: A person arranging blocks on a digital calendar
blocks.caption: Time blocking turns your task list into appointments with yourself.

blocks.text: How to block a day

items: Check your planned capacity from Module 1, Lesson 3 (for example, about 5 hours).
Put fixed meetings and duties into Google Calendar first.
Choose your most important task and block 60 to 120 minutes for it in your best-energy hours. Name the block with the action, such as "Write board report section 2", not just "Work".
Add one or two blocks for batched shallow work, such as "Messages and email" at 11:30 a.m. and 3:30 p.m.
Leave a buffer block in the afternoon for things that come up.
Use a different colour for deep work, shallow batches and meetings so you can see the balance at a glance.

blocks.text: Useful Google Calendar features: you can make a block **repeat** every weekday; set notifications 5 minutes before a block starts; and on many work or school Google accounts you can create a **Focus time** event, which can automatically decline meeting invitations during that block. If you have a personal Gmail account, an ordinary event named "Focus: proposal" and marked Busy works as a visible signal to anyone who can see your calendar.
Pomodoro: focus in short sprints

The **Pomodoro Technique** was developed by **Francesco Cirillo** in the late 1980s and named after a tomato-shaped kitchen timer. The basic cycle: choose one task, work on it for 25 minutes without switching, take a short break of about 5 minutes, and after four of these sessions take a longer break of 15 to 30 minutes. Pomodoro works well inside a time block: a 2-hour deep-work block holds about four sessions. If a thought or request interrupts you, write it in your capture inbox and return to the task.

blocks.title: A time-blocked workday (example)
items: 8:30 Plan the day
9:00 Deep work (4 Pomodoros)
11:30 Messages batch
1:00 Meetings block
3:30 Messages batch
4:15 Buffer and shutdown
blocks.caption: Deep work comes first, shallow work is grouped into batches and the day ends with a buffer.

blocks.text: Batching: group similar tasks

Each time you switch between different kinds of task, you lose time getting back into the first one. **Batching** means doing similar tasks together in one block: all calls, all payments and transfers, all invoices, all social media posts. For a small business, a weekly batch might be "Monday 4 p.m.: pay suppliers and record transfers on Moniepoint or Opay" rather than paying one supplier at a time throughout the week.

blocks.title: Worked example: blocking a sales manager's Wednesday
blocks.context: For example, Chioma is a sales manager at a distribution company in Abuja. Her capacity is about 5 hours. On Wednesday she must prepare a monthly sales review, approve 12 expense claims and handle customer calls.
steps: Fixed items: team meeting 1:00 to 2:00 p.m. and a client visit 2:30 to 3:30 p.m. go into Google Calendar first.
Deep block: 9:00 to 11:00 a.m. "Prepare monthly sales review", run as four 25-minute Pomodoros with 5-minute breaks.
Batch 1: 11:15 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. "Calls and messages". She tells her team she will return calls in that slot.
Batch 2: 3:45 to 4:30 p.m. "Approve expense claims": all 12 at once, about 3 to 4 minutes each.
Buffer: 4:30 to 5:00 p.m. for anything that came up, then a 5-minute shutdown to plan Thursday.
blocks.result: Chioma finishes the sales review by 11 a.m. instead of late at night, approves all claims in one sitting and still handles every call, just in a planned slot.

blocks.text: Protecting the block

items: Before the block starts, open only the file or materials you need and close other tabs.
Put the phone face down or out of reach, with notifications paused (Lesson 3 shows how).
If you share an office or shop, tell colleagues the time you will be free, for example "I am finishing the report until 11, I will come to you then".
Start on time. A block that begins 20 minutes late is a smaller block.

blocks.title: When the plan breaks
blocks.text: It will. A power cut, an urgent client or a sick child can wreck a morning. Do not abandon the method. Take two minutes to re-block the rest of the day: move the deep task to the next free block and drop or postpone the lowest-value item. A re-planned day is still a planned day.

takeaways: A task with a time slot is far more likely to get done.
Block your most important task first, in your best-energy hours.
Pomodoro: 25 minutes focus, short break, longer break after four.
Batch similar shallow tasks and re-block when the day changes.

activity.title: Time-block three days
steps: Block tomorrow in Google Calendar: fixed items, one deep-work block, two batch blocks and a buffer.
Colour-code deep, shallow and meetings.
Run your deep block as Pomodoros, using a phone timer, and write interruptions in your capture inbox.
At the end of each day, note what you finished and re-block the next day.
Repeat for three working days.
activity.evidence: Screenshots of three time-blocked days in Google Calendar and a note of how many Pomodoros you completed each day.

lessons.title: Taming email and WhatsApp interruptions
objectives: Set up Gmail filters, labels and snooze to reduce inbox noise
Use WhatsApp mute, archive and WhatsApp Business tools to control interruptions
Process messages in batches with a simple decision rule
Agree a response-time expectation with your team or customers

blocks.text: For many workers in Nigeria, WhatsApp is where work happens: staff groups, client chats, supplier updates and payment confirmations, all mixed with family and church groups. Email adds another stream. Each notification invites you to switch tasks. The goal of this lesson is not to ignore people, but to **decide when** you deal with messages, so that your best hours go to your most important work.

blocks.name: inbox-cleanup
blocks.alt: A person sorting and clearing items from an inbox
blocks.caption: You decide when to process messages, so they stop deciding your day.

blocks.text: The four Ds for every message
When you open your inbox in a batch, make one decision per message, then move on. Do not read a message, close it and leave it for later without deciding.

blocks.title: The four Ds of message processing
items: Delete or archive it
Do it (under two minutes)
Delegate it to the right person
Defer it to a task or snooze
blocks.caption: Every message leaves the inbox with one of four decisions, so nothing sits unread and undecided.

blocks.text: Gmail tools that save time

items: **Filters**: in Gmail on a computer, use the search bar options to create a filter, for example all emails from a supplier's address get a label "Suppliers" and skip the inbox, or newsletters are marked as read and archived.
**Labels**: like folders, but one email can have several. Keep them few, such as Clients, Suppliers, Finance, Reference.
**Snooze**: hides an email until a date and time you choose, then returns it to the top of your inbox. Use it for messages you cannot act on yet.
**Schedule send**: write a reply now and choose when it is delivered, for example 8 a.m. tomorrow, so you do not train people to expect replies late at night.
**Templates**: save replies you send often (turn them on in Gmail settings under Advanced), such as your price list response or meeting confirmation.
**Add to Tasks**: from the Gmail side panel, turn an email into a Google Task so it joins your task system.

blocks.text: WhatsApp tools that save time

items: **Mute**: mute busy groups for 8 hours, 1 week or always. Muted chats still receive messages; you just are not interrupted.
**Archive**: move chats out of the main list. With the "keep chats archived" setting on, they stay archived when new messages arrive.
**Pin**: pin your most important work chats to the top so they are easy to check during a batch.
**Notifications**: turn off message previews and group notifications in WhatsApp settings if you want quiet focus time.

**WhatsApp Business** (free app for businesses): **quick replies** for frequent answers (typed with a shortcut beginning with "/"), an **away message** outside business hours, a **greeting message** for new customers, **labels** such as "New order" or "Paid", and a **catalogue** so customers can see products without asking you each time.

blocks.text: Your phone helps too. On Android, **Digital Wellbeing** has a Focus mode that pauses chosen apps; on iPhone, **Focus** lets you choose which people and apps can notify you, so calls from your manager or your children's school still come through while group chats wait.

blocks.title: Worked example: a caterer takes back her mornings
blocks.context: For example, Bukola runs a catering business in Lagos. Her baseline showed 28 WhatsApp interruptions a day and only 30 minutes of focused menu planning and costing.
steps: She moves customer chats to WhatsApp Business and creates 5 quick replies: price list, delivery areas, how to pay, order deadline and menu for the week.
She labels chats "New enquiry", "Order confirmed" and "Paid", so she can see where each customer is without scrolling.
She mutes 6 non-urgent groups for "always" and checks them once a day at 4 p.m.

She sets three message batches: 8:00, 12:30 and 4:00 p.m., about 30 minutes each, and adds a line to her WhatsApp Business profile: "Messages answered at 8am, 12:30pm and 4pm. For same-day emergencies, please call."
During her 9:00 to 11:00 a.m. focus block she switches on Focus mode, allowing calls only.
blocks.result: After two weeks her interruptions fall to about 6 a day (mostly calls), she gets close to 2 focused hours each morning, and customers still receive answers within a few hours. Quick replies cut her typing in each batch.

blocks.text: Agree response times

Batching works best when people know what to expect. Agree a simple rule with your manager and team, such as "WhatsApp messages answered within 3 working hours; anything truly urgent, please call". For customers, state your hours and response times on your WhatsApp Business profile and in your away message. Clear expectations remove the pressure to reply instantly, and they make you look more organised, not less available.

blocks.title: Watch for message scams
blocks.text: Batching messages also gives you time to check them calmly. Be suspicious of urgent payment requests, new account numbers sent by "suppliers", or messages claiming to be from your bank. Confirm by calling a number you already know, and never share OTPs or PINs on WhatsApp.

takeaways: Decide when you process messages; do not let notifications decide.
Give every message one of four Ds: delete, do, delegate, defer.
Gmail filters, snooze, schedule send and templates cut inbox time.
WhatsApp mute, archive and Business quick replies, labels and away messages cut interruptions.

activity.title: Set up message control
steps: Create at least two Gmail filters or labels and one template, or (if you use WhatsApp mostly) five WhatsApp Business quick replies.
Mute or archive every non-urgent group.
Choose two or three message batch times and add them to Google Calendar as repeating events.
Tell your team or customers your batch times and how to reach you for real emergencies.
For three days, tally interruptions again using the codes from Module 1.
activity.evidence: Screenshots of your filters or quick replies, your muted groups and batch-time calendar events, plus your new three-day interruption tally.

quiz.q: Grace's list contains the item "Lagos warehouse". Following GTD, what should she do with it?
options: Leave it as it is, she will remember what it means
Delete it, because it is too vague
Turn it into a project and write a clear next action such as "Call Tunde to book a warehouse viewing"
Put it in Google Calendar for today
quiz.explain: Vague items stall. If it needs more than one step it is a project, and it needs a next action that starts with a verb.

quiz.q: Emeka promised to send a printer quote by Friday. Where does this belong in the task system?
options: Waiting-for list, with the date she asked
quiz.explain: Things other people owe you go on a waiting-for list with the date, so you can follow up in your weekly review.

quiz.q: Chioma has a 2-hour deep-work block. Using the standard Pomodoro cycle, about how many focus sessions fit?
quiz.explain: 25 minutes of work plus about 5 minutes of break is 30 minutes per session, so about four sessions fit in 2 hours.

quiz.q: Which is an example of batching?
options: Paying all supplier transfers in one Monday afternoon block
Replying to each message as soon as it arrives
Working on three reports at the same time
quiz.explain: Batching groups similar tasks into one block to avoid repeated switching.

quiz.q: A customer sends Bukola the same delivery-area question she answers ten times a day. What WhatsApp Business tool saves the most time?
quiz.explain: A quick reply sends a saved answer with a short shortcut, cutting repeated typing.

quiz.q: A message from a "supplier" says their account number has changed and payment is urgent today. What should she do?
options: Pay immediately to keep the relationship
Forward it to her staff group
Call the supplier on a number she already has to confirm before paying
quiz.explain: Changed account details plus urgency is a common scam pattern. Confirm through a known number before sending money.

modules.title: Quality and Evidence: Delegation, Sustainable Pace and the Weekly Review
modules.overview: A good system must work week after week without wearing you out. This module covers delegating work clearly, recognising and preventing burnout at work, and running a weekly review with a few simple numbers that show whether your methods are really working.

lessons.title: Delegating work clearly and following up
objectives: Decide which tasks to delegate and which to keep
Write a clear delegation brief covering outcome, deadline, resources and authority
Choose a suitable level of authority for the person and task
Follow up using check-ins and a waiting-for list without micromanaging

blocks.text: If you are a supervisor, a business owner with even one assistant, or a team member who shares work with colleagues, you cannot do everything yourself. **Delegation** means handing a task to someone else while you stay responsible for the result. Done well, it frees your time for deep work on your key results and helps others grow. Done badly, it produces wrong work, rework and frustration, and many people then decide "it is faster to do it myself".

blocks.name: task-brief
blocks.alt: Two people discussing a written task brief
blocks.caption: A clear brief is the difference between delegation that works and rework.

blocks.text: What to delegate

Go through your Next actions list and your Module 1 log. Good candidates to delegate are tasks that are repeated often, that someone else can learn, or that someone else can do well enough at lower cost. Tasks to keep are those only you can do: decisions that need your authority, sensitive conversations, and the deep work tied to your key results.

head: Delegate (for example)
Keep (for example)
rows: Daily stock count and reorder list
Choosing new suppliers and negotiating prices
Posting the week's products on the business page
Booking venues and sending meeting reminders
First draft of routine monthly report tables
Final review and sign-off of a donor report

blocks.text: Write a delegation brief
Most failed delegation is a briefing problem. Give the brief in writing (a short WhatsApp message, email or Google Doc) even if you also explain it in person. Cover five points:

items: **Outcome**: what "done" looks like. "A list of all items below reorder level, with quantities and supplier, in the shared sheet" is clearer than "check the stock".
**Deadline**: a date and time, plus any check-in point.
**Resources**: files, money, contacts, templates or examples of good past work.
**Authority**: what they can decide alone and what needs your approval, such as "you can spend up to 20,000 naira without asking me".
**Check-in**: when and how you will review progress.

blocks.text: Match authority to experience

A new staff member may need a clear method and approval before acting. An experienced colleague may only need the outcome and deadline. A useful way to think about it is a ladder of authority, from "Do exactly this" to "Decide and act, tell me afterwards". Choose the rung for each task and person, and say it out loud so there is no confusion.

blocks.title: Ladder of delegated authority
items: Decide, act, report later
Decide, act, tell me now
Recommend, I decide
Investigate and report back
Do exactly as instructed
blocks.caption: Start lower for new people and new tasks, and move up the ladder as trust and skill grow.

blocks.title: Worked example: delegating weekly stock control
blocks.context: For example, Esther owns a provisions shop in Ilorin and spends about 3 hours every Saturday counting stock and preparing orders. Her shop assistant, Kunle, has worked with her for 8 months.
steps: She writes a brief on WhatsApp: outcome (reorder list in a shared Google Sheet with item, quantity left, quantity to order, supplier), deadline (Saturday 1 p.m.), resources (the sheet template and supplier price list), authority (Kunle prepares the list; Esther approves and pays).
Week 1: they count together and she shows how she decides reorder quantities. Authority level: do exactly as instructed.
Weeks 2 and 3: Kunle counts alone; Esther checks 10 items at random. Two errors in week 2, none in week 3.
Week 4: she moves him up to "recommend, I decide". Her time on stock falls to about 30 minutes of checking and approval.
She records the task on her Waiting-for list every Saturday until the habit is reliable.
blocks.result: Esther saves about 2.5 hours each week, which she uses for a new Saturday deep-work block: building relationships with two nearby schools for bulk orders.

blocks.text: Following up without micromanaging

Agree check-ins in advance so they feel normal, not like suspicion: for a one-week task, a short check halfway is usually enough. At the check-in, ask what is done, what is blocking progress and what help is needed. When the work comes back, give specific feedback: what was good, and one thing to change next time. Resist redoing the work yourself; instead, explain the gap and let the person fix it, so they learn and the task stays delegated.

blocks.title: Delegation is not dumping
blocks.text: Hand over the task with the training, tools and authority to do it, and give credit when it is done well. Delegating only unpleasant work with no support, or taking back tasks at the first mistake, destroys trust. Also never delegate access to your bank app, PINs or passwords; use separate staff logins or approval limits where your bank or payment app provides them.

blocks.title: Upward delegation
blocks.text: If a colleague keeps bringing problems back for you to solve, ask "What do you recommend?" before giving your answer. Over time this builds their judgement and keeps the task with them.

takeaways: Delegate repeated, learnable tasks; keep decisions and key deep work.
A brief covers outcome, deadline, resources, authority and check-in.
Match authority to experience and move up as trust grows.
Track delegated tasks on your Waiting-for list.

activity.title: Delegate one real task
steps: Choose one repeated task from your log that someone else could learn.
Write a five-point delegation brief and agree the authority level.
Hand it over and add it to your Waiting-for list with the check-in date.
Review the result at the check-in and give specific feedback.
Estimate the hours per week you saved.
activity.evidence: A copy of your written brief, a note of the check-in result and your estimate of time saved.

lessons.title: Avoiding burnout: sustainable pace at work
objectives: Describe burnout using the World Health Organization's three dimensions
Recognise early warning signs in yourself and your team
Use workload conversations and shutdown routines to protect your pace
Know when and where to seek help

blocks.text: A productivity system that pushes you to do more and more can make things worse. Productivity is meant to help you do the right work and then **stop**. In 2019 the **World Health Organization (WHO)** included burn-out in the 11th revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11) as an **occupational phenomenon**, not a medical condition. WHO describes it as resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed.

blocks.name: quitting-time
blocks.alt: A person closing a laptop and leaving work at the end of the day
blocks.caption: A clear end to the workday is part of a productive system, not a break from it.

blocks.text: The three dimensions
WHO describes burn-out with three dimensions. Knowing them helps you notice it early, in yourself or in a colleague.

blocks.title: How unmanaged work stress builds burnout
items: Overload and long hours
Exhaustion
Mental distance and cynicism
Reduced effectiveness
More hours to catch up
blocks.caption: When the response to falling effectiveness is simply more hours, the cycle feeds itself; breaking it needs a change in workload or recovery.

items: **Exhaustion**: feelings of energy depletion. Rest at the weekend no longer restores you.
**Mental distance**: increased mental distance from your job, or feelings of negativism or cynicism about it. You stop caring about work that used to matter.
**Reduced professional efficacy**: you feel less effective and accomplish less, even when you work longer.

blocks.text: Early warning signs to watch

items: Regularly working late or at weekends just to keep up, not for a short, planned peak.
Answering work messages in bed or during family time because you fear falling behind.
Dreading Monday from Saturday evening.
Making more small mistakes and taking longer over simple tasks.
Skipping meals, breaks or exercise because there is "no time".

blocks.text: Practical protections

**1. A shutdown routine.** End the workday with 10 minutes to capture loose ends into your inbox, check tomorrow's calendar and choose the first task. Then stop. Cal Newport recommends a fixed ritual like this so that work stops occupying your mind in the evening. If you work from home, close the laptop or put the work phone away as a clear signal.

**2. Use your capacity number.** When a new request arrives and your week is already full to capacity, something must move. Ask your manager which task should give way rather than silently adding hours: "I can take on the audit preparation. To do it by Friday, I would move the training plan to next week. Which do you prefer?"

**3. Protect breaks and leave.** Short breaks between Pomodoros and a real lunch break restore attention. Plan annual leave early and set an out-of-office reply in Gmail (and an away message in WhatsApp Business) so you can actually rest.

**4. Look after the basics.** Sleep, regular meals, water and some movement during the day are not luxuries for a busy person; they are what attention runs on. A short walk between blocks or stretching during a Pomodoro break helps more than scrolling through your phone.

**5. If you lead a team, watch your team too.** Notice colleagues who are always online late, who have become withdrawn or who are making unusual mistakes. Ask privately how they are coping with their workload, and review how work is shared before pushing for more output.

blocks.title: Worked example: a workload conversation
blocks.context: For example, Adaeze is an accountant at a mid-sized company in Enugu. For six weeks she has worked until 9 p.m. most days. Her weekly review shows she completed only 2 of her 5 planned priorities last week, and she feels drained every morning.
steps: She lists her current commitments with estimated hours: month-end close (14), payroll (6), audit preparation (10), supplier reconciliations (8), ad hoc requests (about 8). Total: 46 hours against a capacity of about 32 hours.
She identifies tasks that could move or be shared: supplier reconciliations could go to the junior accountant with a brief; audit preparation could start a week later.
She books 20 minutes with her manager and presents the list: "I have about 46 hours of work and 32 hours of real capacity. I suggest these two changes. Which would you prefer?"
They agree to delegate reconciliations and move one audit deadline. She sets a shutdown routine at 5:30 p.m. and a Focus block every morning.
blocks.result: Her planned work falls to about 34 hours. Within three weeks she is leaving by 6 p.m. on most days and completing 4 of 5 weekly priorities.

blocks.title: When to seek help
blocks.text: If exhaustion, low mood, poor sleep or loss of interest continue for weeks, or affect your health and relationships, speak to a doctor or a qualified counsellor, and to your HR department if your workplace has one. If you ever feel unable to cope or have thoughts of harming yourself, contact a health professional or emergency services immediately and tell someone you trust.

takeaways: WHO describes burn-out by exhaustion, mental distance and reduced effectiveness.
Working more hours to catch up often feeds the cycle.
Use a shutdown routine and your capacity number to protect your pace.
Raise workload with options, not just complaints; seek help early.

activity.title: Build your sustainable-pace plan
steps: Score yourself 1 to 5 on each WHO dimension for the last month.
Write a 10-minute shutdown routine and set a repeating calendar reminder for it.
List your current commitments with estimated hours and compare with your capacity.
If you are over capacity, write two options to discuss with your manager, client or partner.
Practise the routine for five working days.
activity.evidence: Your self-score, written shutdown routine, commitments-versus-capacity list and a note on the five days.

lessons.title: The weekly review and a simple productivity scorecard
objectives: Run a 30 to 45 minute weekly review of your work system
Track four simple productivity measures in a weekly scorecard
Interpret your numbers and choose one adjustment for the next week
Check progress on your OKR each week

blocks.text: Systems decay. Lists fill with old items, the calendar drifts back to reactive days, and quick replies go out of date. David Allen calls the **weekly review** the critical success factor of GTD, the step that keeps the whole system trusted. In this lesson you combine the weekly review with a short scorecard so that you have evidence, not just feelings, about whether your methods are working.

blocks.name: progress-tracking
blocks.alt: A person reviewing progress charts and a checklist
blocks.caption: A weekly review turns your methods into evidence you can improve.

blocks.text: The weekly review in three parts
Choose a fixed slot, such as Friday at 3:30 p.m. or Monday at 8 a.m., and block it in Google Calendar as a repeating event. Allen groups the review into three parts:

items: **Get clear**: empty your capture inbox, Gmail starred items and WhatsApp saved messages. Clarify every item into your lists. Clear your desk and notebook pages.

**Get current**: go through Next actions (tick off finished items, delete dead ones), Waiting for (follow up on anything overdue), Projects (each one has a next action) and the last and next two weeks of your calendar.
**Get creative**: look at your someday list and your OKR. Is there a new idea, opportunity or risk to act on?

blocks.text: Do the review at your desk with your phone, notebook and computer in front of you, so you can empty every inbox in one sitting. Many people like Friday afternoon because the week is fresh in their mind and Monday starts with a ready plan.
Then plan the next week: choose your top three priorities, each linked to a key result, and block time for them in Google Calendar before the week fills up.
Your weekly scorecard
Keep a Google Sheet with one row per week and these columns. The first three come from your Module 1 baseline, so you can compare directly.

head: Measure
How to count it
What it tells you
rows: Whether you plan realistically and protect important work
Deep-work blocks completed (or Pomodoros divided by 2)
One sample day's tally each week
Current number for each key result
Whether the work is moving your goal
Your honest rating of the week

blocks.title: The weekly improvement loop
items: Review the week
Record the scorecard
Find one cause
Adjust one thing
Plan next week
blocks.caption: Change one thing at a time, so the next scorecard shows whether that change helped.

blocks.text: Reading the numbers

items: **Priorities often unfinished, focused hours fine**: you are probably planning more than your capacity. Choose smaller priorities or fewer.
**Focused hours low, interruptions high**: return to Module 2, Lesson 3 and tighten one message habit.
**Everything improving, key result flat**: you are being efficient on the wrong work. Check that your weekly priorities really drive the key result.
**Energy falling for two or more weeks**: reduce load before output falls (Lesson 2).

blocks.title: Worked example: four weeks of scorecards
blocks.context: For example, Funke (the programme officer from Module 1) started with a baseline of 1 focused hour a day, 23 interruptions a day and no clear weekly priorities.
steps: Week 1: priorities 1 of 3, focused hours 6 for the week, interruptions 15, energy 3. Cause: she planned three large reports. Adjustment: break reports into sections.
Week 2: priorities 2 of 3, focused hours 8, interruptions 14, energy 3. Cause: the staff group chat still pulls her in. Adjustment: mute it and check at 12 and 4.
Week 3: priorities 3 of 3, focused hours 9, interruptions 8, energy 4. No major problem; she keeps the system.
Week 4: priorities 3 of 3, focused hours 10, interruptions 7, energy 4. Key result "donor reports submitted on time": 2 of 2 this month.
blocks.result: In four weeks Funke's focused time roughly doubled from her baseline of about 5 hours a week, interruptions fell by about two thirds and she has numbers to show her manager.

blocks.text: Common review mistakes

items: **Skipping it when busy**: busy weeks are when the review matters most, because that is when lists fall out of date. Shorten it to 20 minutes rather than skip it.
**Only reviewing the to-do list**: the calendar, the waiting-for list and the OKR are where many surprises hide.
**Changing everything at once**: if you change three habits together and your numbers improve, you will not know which one helped.
**Judging yourself harshly**: the scorecard is information, not a grade. A bad week tells you what to adjust.

blocks.title: Keep the review short
blocks.text: If your review takes more than an hour, your lists are too long or you are doing work during the review. Note those tasks and do them in the week. A 30-minute review done every week beats a perfect 2-hour review done once a month.

takeaways: The weekly review keeps your system trusted: get clear, get current, get creative.
Track priority completion, focused hours, interruptions, key result progress and energy.
Change one thing per week so you can see its effect.
Compare your scorecard with your Module 1 baseline.

activity.title: Run your first weekly review
steps: Block a repeating 45-minute weekly review in Google Calendar.
Run the three parts: get clear, get current, get creative.
Create your scorecard sheet and fill in this week's row.
Write one cause and one adjustment for next week.
Choose next week's top three priorities and block time for them.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your scorecard sheet with at least one completed week, and your list of next week's top three priorities.

quiz.q: Esther wants to delegate stock counting to Kunle. Which brief is clearest?
options: Do what I normally do on Saturdays
Count all items, put those below reorder level in the shared sheet with quantity and supplier by Saturday 1 p.m.; I approve before ordering
quiz.explain: It states the outcome, deadline, resources (the sheet) and authority (she approves before ordering).

quiz.q: Kunle is new and has never prepared a reorder list. What authority level is most suitable to start?
options: Do exactly as instructed, with a check
Decide and act without telling her
No instructions, he will learn by trying
quiz.explain: New people on new tasks start lower on the ladder and move up as skill and trust grow.

quiz.q: Which set describes the three WHO dimensions of burn-out?
options: Exhaustion, mental distance or cynicism, reduced professional efficacy
Low pay, long commute, bad manager
quiz.explain: WHO's ICD-11 description uses energy depletion or exhaustion, increased mental distance or cynicism, and reduced professional efficacy.

quiz.q: Adaeze has 46 hours of work and about 32 hours of capacity. What is the best next step?
options: Work until 10 p.m. until it is done
Quietly drop tasks without telling anyone
Present her list and two options to her manager and agree what moves
quiz.explain: A workload conversation with options lets her manager choose priorities and keeps her pace sustainable.

quiz.q: Over three weeks Ngozi's focused hours and interruptions improved, but her key result has not moved. What does this suggest?
options: Her weekly priorities may not be the work that drives the key result
quiz.explain: Efficiency on the wrong work does not move goals. Check that the priorities are linked to the key result.

quiz.q: In the weekly review, what does "get current" involve?
options: Updating lists, following up waiting-for items and checking the calendar
Deleting all old tasks without reading them
quiz.explain: Get current means bringing your lists and calendar up to date; get creative is where new ideas come in.

modules.title: Portfolio and Impact: Prove the Change and Plan the Next 90 Days
modules.overview: In the final module you run a two-week improvement experiment against your baseline, present your before-and-after results in a way an employer or client will value, and write a 90-day plan built on a new quarterly OKR so the habits last beyond the course.

lessons.title: Running your two-week productivity experiment
objectives: Write a testable hypothesis about one change to your working method
Run the change for at least two weeks while tracking the same measures as your baseline
Compare results fairly with your baseline
Decide whether to keep, adjust or drop the change

blocks.text: Your capstone asks for a **specific, implemented change tested over at least a week, with an honest before-and-after comparison**. This lesson shows how to make that test fair. You treat your working method like a small experiment: one change, measured the same way as your baseline, long enough to see past one good or bad day. Two weeks is better than one, because the first few days of any new habit are unusual.

blocks.name: progress-data
blocks.alt: Charts comparing results before and after a change
blocks.caption: A fair experiment compares the same measures before and after one change.

blocks.text: Step 1: choose one change
Look at your baseline from Module 1, Lesson 3 and the biggest time drain you named. Choose the method from this course most likely to fix it. One change only, so you can tell whether it worked.

head: If your biggest drain is
Test one of these changes
rows: Three message batches a day with mute, Focus mode and quick replies
All meetings moved into two afternoon blocks; mornings blocked for deep work
Daily top-three plus a GTD task system and weekly review
Too much work you could hand over
Delegating one repeated task with a written brief
Starting deep work late or not at all
A 9 a.m. deep-work block run as four Pomodoros

blocks.text: Step 2: write a hypothesis

A hypothesis is a prediction you can check. Use this pattern: "If I [change], then [measure] will move from [baseline] to [target] within [time]." For example: "If I batch WhatsApp into three slots a day, my interruptions will fall from 23 to under 10 a day, and my focused hours will rise from 1 to 2 a day, within two weeks." Write it down before you start, so you cannot quietly change the target later.
Step 3: run and record

items: Set up everything the change needs on day 0 (calendar blocks, filters, quick replies, the delegation brief).
Tell the people affected, such as your manager, team or regular customers.
Track the same measures as your baseline. At minimum, tally interruptions on three sample days each week and record focused hours daily.
Keep a short daily note: what worked, what got in the way, anything unusual (a public holiday, a power outage, a sick day).
Do not add a second change in the middle. Write new ideas on your someday list for later.

blocks.title: The two-week experiment
items: Baseline numbers
One change plus hypothesis
Run for two weeks
Compare same measures
Keep, adjust or drop
blocks.caption: The baseline and the result are measured in the same way, so the comparison is fair.

blocks.text: Step 4: compare fairly

Put the baseline and the experiment side by side in a table. Use averages per day or per week, not your best day. Note anything unusual that may have affected the numbers, such as a quiet week after a public holiday or a busy end-of-month period. If the experiment weeks were not typical, say so; honesty here is what makes your evidence believable.

blocks.title: Worked example: testing meeting blocks
blocks.context: For example, Rukayat is a project coordinator at a construction firm in Abuja. Her baseline showed 6 meetings a day spread from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., 0.5 focused hours a day and 2 of 5 weekly priorities completed.
steps: Hypothesis: "If I move internal meetings into 1 p.m. to 4 p.m. and block 9 to 11:30 a.m. for deep work, my focused hours will rise from 0.5 to at least 2 a day within two weeks."
Day 0: she sets a repeating Focus time block from 9 to 11:30 a.m. in Google Calendar and messages her team: "From Monday, please book meetings with me between 1 and 4 p.m."
Week 1: focused hours average 1.6 a day; two site meetings still land in the morning because a client could only meet then.
Week 2: she offers the client two afternoon slots; focused hours average 2.2 a day. Weekly priorities completed: 4 of 5.
Comparison: focused hours from 0.5 to an average of 1.9 over two weeks; priorities from 2 of 5 to 4 of 5. Unusual factor: week 1 included a site inspection.
blocks.result: Rukayat keeps the change and adjusts it: client meetings are allowed in the morning once a week. She has clear, honest numbers for her capstone.

blocks.title: A failed experiment is still evidence
blocks.text: If your numbers did not improve, you have still learned something real. Write down why you think it did not work and what you would adjust. A clear account of a change that did not work, followed by a better second attempt, shows more skill than a claim that everything worked perfectly.

takeaways: Test one change at a time against your baseline.
Write a hypothesis with a measure, a target and a time frame before you start.
Track the same measures in the same way for at least two weeks.
Compare averages honestly and note unusual factors.

activity.title: Launch your experiment
steps: Choose one change linked to your biggest time drain.
Write your hypothesis using the pattern in this lesson.
Set everything up on day 0 and tell the people affected.
Track your measures daily for two weeks with a short daily note.
Build a before-and-after table and write keep, adjust or drop.
activity.evidence: Your written hypothesis, daily tracking notes and the completed before-and-after table.

lessons.title: Presenting your results to a manager, client or employer
objectives: Write a one-page before-and-after productivity report
Translate time saved into value for an employer or business
Describe your productivity skill with evidence in a CV line or interview answer
Propose a team improvement based on your results

blocks.text: Saying "I am very organised" is a claim. Showing "I cut interruptions from 23 to 7 a day and now submit donor reports on time" is evidence. Employers, clients and partners trust evidence. This lesson shows you how to turn your experiment into a short report and a few sentences you can use in appraisals, job interviews or conversations with business partners.

blocks.name: report
blocks.alt: A person presenting a short report with charts
blocks.caption: A one-page report turns your experiment into evidence others can trust.

blocks.text: The one-page report
Keep it to one page, in Google Docs or on paper. Use these five headings:

items: **Problem**: what was not working, in one or two sentences, with your baseline numbers.
**Change**: the one method you tested and how you set it up.
**Results**: a before-and-after table with your measures.
**Value**: what the result means for the work, such as reports on time, faster customer replies or more sales visits.
**Next step**: what you will keep, adjust or try next, and any request (for example, a team agreement on message times).

blocks.text: Turn time into value

Managers and business owners think in results and money. Connect your hours to what they make possible. If you freed 5 hours a week, what did those hours produce? More client visits, a finished proposal, a training delivered, fewer errors? For a business owner, you can estimate value directly: if each extra sales visit brings, on average, one order in four, and an order earns about 10,000 naira profit (approximate), then 4 extra visits a week is roughly one extra order, or about 10,000 naira a week. Always label estimates as estimates.

blocks.title: Weak claim and strong evidence
items: Weak claim
Strong evidence
right: Cut interruptions from 23 to 7 a day
Focused hours up from 1 to 2 daily
Quick replies cut daily messaging time
blocks.caption: Strong evidence names the change, the measure and the result.

blocks.title: Worked example: a report and a CV line
blocks.context: For example, Bukola, the Lagos caterer from Module 2, wants to show a potential business partner how she manages the workload, and to update her CV for a corporate catering contract.
steps: Problem: "28 WhatsApp interruptions a day; 30 minutes of focused menu planning daily; missed two costing deadlines last month."
Change: "WhatsApp Business with 5 quick replies, labels and three message batches a day; Focus mode 9 to 11 a.m."
Results table: interruptions 28 to 6 a day; focused planning 0.5 to nearly 2 hours a day; costing deadlines missed 2 to 0.
Value: "Every quote now goes out within one working day, and I have time to plan menus for larger corporate events."
CV line: "Redesigned customer messaging with WhatsApp Business quick replies and scheduled response times, reducing daily interruptions by about 80 percent while keeping same-day replies."
blocks.result: Bukola has a one-page report she can share and a CV line backed by real numbers she can explain if asked.

blocks.text: Tips for presenting numbers

items: **Use simple comparisons**: "from 23 to 7 a day" is clearer than percentages alone. Give both if you like.
**Show the time frame**: say how long you measured, such as "two-week test against a three-day baseline".
**Round sensibly**: "nearly 2 hours" is fine when your log shows 1.9. Do not round in your own favour.
**Add one picture**: a simple bar chart in Google Sheets of before and after for your main measure helps a busy reader.
**Lead with the result**: put the headline number in the first line of your report or message.

blocks.text: Answering interview questions

When asked "How do you manage your time?" or "Tell me about a time you handled a heavy workload", use the **STAR** structure, a common format for interview answers: **Situation** (the context), **Task** (what you needed to achieve), **Action** (what you did, step by step) and **Result** (what changed, with numbers). Your experiment fits it exactly. Practise saying it in under two minutes.
Suggesting a team improvement

If your change worked, others may benefit. Propose it carefully: share your own results first, suggest a small trial (for example, a two-week team agreement that the staff group chat is for announcements only, with replies batched at 12 and 4), and agree how you will all judge it. A suggestion backed by your own numbers is far more persuasive than a general complaint about too many messages.

Use your appraisal too. Many organisations hold mid-year or annual reviews where you are asked what you achieved. Bring your one-page report and scorecard. Numbers about how you improved your own working method show initiative, and they give your manager something specific to write about you.

blocks.title: Keep it honest and confidential
blocks.text: Report your real numbers, including what did not improve. Do not include colleagues' names, client details or confidential figures in a report you share outside your organisation. Ask your manager before sharing work data publicly, for example in a LinkedIn post.

takeaways: Evidence beats claims: name the change, the measure and the result.
Use a one-page report: problem, change, results, value, next step.
Translate hours saved into results or money, labelled as estimates.
Use STAR for interview answers and propose team trials with your own data.

activity.title: Write your one-page report
steps: Draft your report under the five headings using your experiment data.
Add a value sentence that connects time saved to a result.
Write one CV or appraisal line with a number in it.
Prepare a two-minute STAR answer and say it aloud once.
Share the report with your manager, a colleague or a mentor and note their feedback.
activity.evidence: Your one-page report, CV line and a note of the feedback you received.

lessons.title: Your 90-day productivity plan and certification checklist
objectives: Write a new quarterly OKR for your next 90 days
Schedule the habits that keep your system running
Plan how to recover when habits slip
Check your capstone evidence against the certification checklist

blocks.text: A new way of working can fade within weeks if nothing holds it in place. The capstone asks for a **90-day plan** naming your next priority-setting or time-drain adjustment. Ninety days matches a business quarter, the same period used for OKRs, so it is long enough to make real progress and short enough to stay focused. This lesson helps you build that plan and check your evidence before the final quiz.

blocks.name: master-plan
blocks.alt: A person standing in front of a large plan with milestones
blocks.caption: A 90-day plan keeps your new habits in place after the course ends.

blocks.text: Part 1: set your next OKR

Score the OKR you wrote in Module 1, Lesson 2 from 0 to 1 for each key result (for example, 30 repeat customers out of a target of 40 is 0.75). Then write the next quarter's OKR. Use what you learned: if you set too many key results, choose fewer; if a key result was really an activity, rewrite it as an outcome.
Part 2: choose your next time-drain target

Look at your latest scorecard. Your first drain may now be under control. What is the next biggest one? It might be meetings, unclear handovers from your manager, a task you should delegate or your own late start. Name it and choose one method from this course to test in the first month of the plan, using the same experiment approach as Lesson 1.
Part 3: schedule the keeper habits

head: Habit
When
Where it lives
rows: Daily plan: top three and first block
Two or three set times a day
Repeating Calendar events, WhatsApp Business away message
Repeating Calendar event and Google Sheet
Monthly, in the weekly review closest to month end

blocks.title: Your 90-day plan
items: Week 1: new OKR set
Weeks 2 to 5: test next change
Week 6: mid-point OKR check
Weeks 7 to 12: build on results
Week 13: score and reset
blocks.caption: The plan follows one quarter, with a mid-point check and a scoring session at the end.

blocks.text: Part 4: plan for slips

Habits slip during busy seasons, illness, travel or a new job. Decide now what you will do: "If I miss my weekly review two weeks in a row, I will do a 20-minute version on the next Monday morning." "If interruptions go back above 15 a day, I will restart my three message batches." A plan that expects slips is more likely to survive them.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 90-day plan
blocks.context: For example, Grace, the operations manager from Module 2, finishes the course in late September and plans October to December.
steps: Score last quarter's OKR: key result 1 (on-time deliveries 95 percent): reached 92 percent, score about 0.97; key result 2 (customer complaints under 10 a month): 12 in the last month, score lower; key result 3 (new route plan live): done, score 1.

New objective: "Make our deliveries reliable through the December peak." Key results: complaints under 10 a month in October, November and December; on-time deliveries 95 percent; two dispatch supervisors trained to plan routes.
Next time-drain target: daily phone calls from drivers asking for directions. Test: a shared route sheet each morning, from week 2.
Keeper habits: all six from the table, entered as repeating events on 1 October.
Slip plan: during the December peak, the weekly review shrinks to 20 minutes but is not skipped.
blocks.result: Grace has a one-page plan with a scored past quarter, a new OKR, one experiment, scheduled habits and a slip plan, ready for her capstone.

blocks.text: Certification checklist

items: Three-day baseline log with the four numbers and a named time drain (Module 1).
Written OKR and a scored version at the end (Modules 1 and 4).
Screenshots of your task lists, time-blocked days and message controls (Module 2).
Delegation brief or workload plan, and at least two weekly scorecards (Module 3).
Experiment hypothesis, tracking notes and before-and-after table (Module 4, Lesson 1).
One-page report and 90-day plan (Module 4, Lessons 2 and 3).

blocks.text: Before you submit, read your evidence as if you were the assessor. Could a stranger see what you changed, how you measured it and what happened? If a number appears in your report, can they find where it came from in your log or scorecard? Fill any gaps now; it is much easier than remembering details months later.

blocks.title: Keep your evidence together
blocks.text: Create one Google Drive folder named "Productivity course evidence" and save every screenshot, sheet and document there as you go. It makes your capstone submission quick and gives you a portfolio to show employers or clients later.

takeaways: A 90-day plan matches a business quarter and an OKR cycle.
Score your old OKR, then write a sharper new one.
Schedule keeper habits as repeating events, not intentions.
